Step 7 · build · the unit's argued pairs, both readings sourced, neither coloured, never marked right

Two questions the evidence leaves open

A claim with two readings is a card, never a tick.

argument · contested · F1.13-C04 · inventory a-cobalt-mine · station 2, Blue before China

Which mine gave the blue?

reading one

Qamsar, near Kashan: "the most cited source". Abu'l-Qasim's treatise of 1301 places lâjvard there, and Cleveland's record for the jar says its cobalt came from Iran, likely from Kashan.

The case: a written source of the period names the place, and the jar's holder follows it. F1.13-C04 · F1.13-C02 · f13-e-abulqasim

a position, not an answer
reading two

Anarak, or more than one source: deposits near Anarak, 200 km east of Kashan. Jiang et al. (2020) propose, in their discussion, that ores from the Anarak mining district, "rather than those originating from Qamsar, Kashan as previously thought", "might have served as one of the most likely sources"; Colomban et al. (2021) read the trace elements.

The case: the geochemistry of the pigment in the wares, read against the deposits; the Anarak reading verified at source 3 October 2026. F1.13-C04 · Colomban et al. 2021 · Jiang et al. 2020

a position, not an answer

What would settle it: a geochemical review (research.md). On the lane chart the mine places no tick; the treatise's year is the only tick, and the Xuande wares tested for imported cobalt, 1426–35, are a bar in the materials lane. f13-e-xuande · F1.13-C03

argument · interpretive · F1.13-C14 · inventory a-demand-routes · station 5, Across the sand

Did demand make the routes, or routes the goods?

reading one

Demand for silk, porcelain and gold built and kept the routes. The goods came first; the roads, the sailings and the caravans followed where buyers were.

The case: the course's own argument, read against the canon's Silk Roads and Indian Ocean rows. F1.13-C14 · NET001 · NET005

a position, not an answer
reading two

Routes already there, the monsoon sailing, the caravans, the oases and the ports, made such goods possible and shaped them. What became a good was decided by what the route could carry.

The case: the course's own argument, read against the same canon rows; both readings are interpretive and neither is a record. F1.13-C14 · NET001 · NET005

a position, not an answer

The lecture poses it at station 5, after the gold has crossed the sand; the card is offered after the evidence and never before it. Nothing on the lane chart depends on either reading.
